def: To make someone agree to do something by giving reasons.
ex: It took an hour, but I finally persuaded my boss to let me work from home.
nat: She tried to persuade him to apply for the job, but he said no.

mis.bad: I persuaded that he was right.
mis.good: I convinced him that he was right.
mis.why: Persuade is for getting someone to act (persuade him to leave); for belief with "that", use convince.

def: To make someone believe that something is true.
ex: Her honest speech convinced me that the project was worth the risk.
nat: I'm not convinced this is the best plan.

mis.bad: I am convinced of that he is right.
mis.good: I am convinced that he is right.
mis.why: Use "convinced of + noun" or "convinced that + clause", never "of that".

def: To suggest something without saying it directly.
ex: I don't mean to imply that you made a mistake, but let's check the numbers.
nat: Her silence seemed to imply that she disagreed.

mis.bad: The job implies me to travel a lot.
mis.good: The job involves a lot of travel.
mis.why: Portuguese "implicar" often means "involve"; English "imply" means to suggest something indirectly.

def: To show that something is especially important.
ex: The teacher emphasized that the exam would cover the whole book.
nat: I want to emphasize how much your help means to us.

mis.bad: She emphasized on the deadline.
mis.good: She emphasized the deadline.
mis.why: Emphasize is transitive: no "on" after it.

def: To say firmly that something must happen or is true.
ex: He insisted on paying for dinner, even though we had agreed to split it.
nat: My sister insists that she locked the door.

mis.bad: He insisted me to stay.
mis.good: He insisted that I stay.
mis.why: After insist, use "on + -ing" or "that + clause", not object + "to".

def: To stop someone while they are speaking or doing something.
ex: Please don't interrupt me while I'm explaining the problem.
nat: Sorry to interrupt, but your taxi is here.

mis.bad: Don't interrupt to me.
mis.good: Don't interrupt me.
mis.why: Interrupt is transitive: no "to" before the person.

def: To pause before doing or saying something because you are unsure.
ex: Don't hesitate to call me if anything goes wrong during the trip.
nat: He hesitated for a moment before answering the question.

mis.bad: Don't hesitate in calling me.
mis.good: Don't hesitate to call me.
mis.why: Hesitate is followed by "to + verb".

def: To communicate an idea or feeling clearly.
ex: It's hard to convey how grateful I am for everything you did.
nat: The photo conveys the loneliness of the city at night.

mis.bad: I want to convey my ideas for the audience.
mis.good: I want to convey my ideas to the audience.
mis.why: Convey takes "to" before the receiver.

def: Fair, sensible, or not extreme.
ex: The restaurant serves excellent food at reasonable prices.
nat: It's reasonable to expect an answer within a week.

mis.bad: The movie was reasonable, nothing special.
mis.good: The movie was okay, nothing special.
mis.why: Portuguese "razoável" can mean "so-so"; English "reasonable" means fair or sensible.

def: Speaking in a very direct way that may sound rude.
ex: To be blunt, your presentation needs a lot more work.
nat: My grandfather is blunt, but he always tells the truth.

mis.bad: He was very blunt to me.
mis.good: He was very blunt with me.
mis.why: Use "blunt with" a person or "blunt about" a topic.

def: Careful not to upset people when you speak.
ex: She gave a tactful answer so that nobody felt offended.
nat: It wasn't very tactful to ask her age.

mis.bad: She was very tactic when she told him.
mis.good: She was very tactful when she told him.
mis.why: "Tactic" is a plan (tática); the adjective for careful, polite behavior is "tactful".

def: Not clear or exact.
ex: His instructions were so vague that nobody knew what to do.
nat: I have a vague memory of meeting her years ago.

mis.bad: He was vague in the details.
mis.good: He was vague about the details.
mis.why: Use "vague about" a topic.

def: Saying the opposite of what you mean to mock or annoy someone.
ex: Don't be so sarcastic; I'm trying to help you.
nat: He made a sarcastic comment about my new haircut.

mis.bad: It was sarcastic that the fire station burned down.
mis.good: It was ironic that the fire station burned down.
mis.why: Sarcastic describes a mocking tone; for an unexpected situation use "ironic".

def: Saying what you think openly, even if people disagree.
ex: She is an outspoken critic of the new tax policy.
nat: My aunt is very outspoken at family dinners.

mis.bad: My brother is very outspoken; he loves parties and meeting people.
mis.good: My brother is very outgoing; he loves parties and meeting people.
mis.why: Outspoken means openly giving strong opinions, not being sociable (extrovertido = outgoing).

def: A reason you give for disagreeing with something.
ex: Does anyone have an objection to moving the meeting to Friday?
nat: There was a strong objection from the neighbors.

mis.bad: I have no objection about the plan.
mis.good: I have no objection to the plan.
mis.why: Objection is followed by "to".

def: A particular way of thinking about a subject.
ex: From my viewpoint, working fewer hours would improve productivity.
nat: It helps to see the problem from another viewpoint.

mis.bad: In my point of view, the plan is bad.
mis.good: From my point of view, the plan is bad.
mis.why: Use "from my point of view", not "in my point of view".

def: A kind remark that shows you admire something.
ex: She gave me a nice compliment about my presentation.
nat: Thank you for the compliment; it made my day.

mis.bad: I did a compliment to him.
mis.good: I paid him a compliment.
mis.why: The natural verbs are "pay" or "give", not "do".

def: A story people share that may not be true.
ex: There is a rumor that the company will close next year.
nat: I don't believe rumors until I see proof.

mis.bad: People are rumoring that he is leaving.
mis.good: There is a rumor that he is leaving. / He is rumored to be leaving.
mis.why: Rumor is mainly a noun; the verb is used only in the passive ("is rumored to").

def: Giving a wrong idea of something.
ex: The advertisement was misleading because it hid the extra fees.
nat: The title is misleading; the book is about cooking.

mis.bad: The ad was mislead.
mis.good: The ad was misleading.
mis.why: Use -ing for the thing that gives a wrong idea; "misled" is the past of mislead (people are misled).

def: To say something again using different words.
ex: Let me rephrase the question so it's easier to answer.
nat: Could you rephrase that? I didn't quite follow.

mis.bad: Can you repeat in other words?
mis.good: Can you rephrase that?
mis.why: Natural ways to ask are "rephrase that" or "put it another way".

def: Money given to a student to pay for education.
ex: She won a scholarship to study engineering in Canada.
nat: He studied in London on a full scholarship.

mis.bad: She studies in a scholarship in Canada.
mis.good: She studies in Canada on a scholarship.
mis.why: A scholarship is financial aid, not a school.

def: The subjects taught in a school or course.
ex: Financial education should be part of the school curriculum.
nat: The new curriculum includes more practical projects.

mis.bad: Send me your curriculum for the job.
mis.good: Send me your resume (or CV) for the job.
mis.why: Curriculum means the courses of study; for a job use "resume" or "CV".

def: Money paid for teaching, especially at a university.
ex: Tuition at private universities has increased every year.
nat: My parents helped me pay the tuition during my first year.

mis.bad: I pay the tuition of English every day.
mis.good: I pay tuition fees for the course.
mis.why: Tuition is the money paid, not the lessons themselves.

def: To officially join a course or school.
ex: I enrolled in an evening course to improve my English.
nat: She enrolled her son in a nearby school.

mis.bad: I matriculated in a course.
mis.good: I enrolled in a course.
mis.why: "Matriculate" is rare in English; use "enroll".

def: A piece of work given to a student or employee.
ex: I have to finish this assignment before midnight.
nat: Our first assignment was to interview a stranger.

mis.bad: I have a work to deliver tomorrow.
mis.good: I have an assignment due tomorrow.
mis.why: "Work" is uncountable; a school or job task is an "assignment".

def: A skill, degree, or exam result needed for a job.
ex: You need a teaching qualification to work in a public school.
nat: Experience matters more than qualifications in this field.

mis.bad: She has many qualifications as a person, very kind.
mis.good: She has the right qualifications for the job.
mis.why: Qualifications are formal skills or certificates, not personal qualities.

def: A short period of work experience, often for students.
ex: He got an internship at a bank during the summer.
nat: Her internship turned into a full-time job.

mis.bad: I made an internship in a bank.
mis.good: I did an internship at a bank.
mis.why: Use "do" an internship, not "make".

def: A job that is available and needs someone to fill it.
ex: The company has a vacancy for a sales assistant.
nat: There are no vacancies at the moment, but we keep CVs on file.

mis.bad: There is a vague at the bank.
mis.good: There is a vacancy at the bank.
mis.why: "Vague" means unclear; a job opening is a "vacancy".

def: Moving to a higher position at work.
ex: After five years, she finally got a promotion to manager.
nat: He's hoping for a promotion before the end of the year.

mis.bad: These shoes are in promotion.
mis.good: These shoes are on sale.
mis.why: "Promotion" at work means a higher position; a lower price is "on sale".

def: To officially leave your job.
ex: He resigned after the company ignored his complaints.
nat: She resigned from her post as head teacher last week.

mis.bad: I asked for dismissal from my job.
mis.good: I resigned from my job.
mis.why: "Dismissal" means being fired; to leave voluntarily, use "resign" or "quit".

def: To stop working permanently, usually because of age.
ex: My father plans to retire when he turns sixty-five.
nat: Many people retire earlier than they expected.

mis.bad: He retired the money from the bank.
mis.good: He took the money out of the bank.
mis.why: "Retire" means to stop working; it does not mean to take something out.

def: An experienced person who gives advice to a less experienced one.
ex: My mentor taught me how to handle difficult clients.
nat: She has been a mentor to many young engineers.

mis.bad: She mentors me since 2020.
mis.good: She has been mentoring me since 2020.
mis.why: With "since" use the present perfect (continuous), not the simple present.

def: Having the skills needed to do something well.
ex: She is a competent engineer who rarely makes mistakes.
nat: You need a competent lawyer for a case like this.

mis.bad: The market is very competent.
mis.good: The market is very competitive.
mis.why: Competent means skilled; "competitive" relates to competition.

def: Giving you satisfaction because it is worthwhile.
ex: Teaching is tiring, but it is also incredibly rewarding.
nat: Volunteering at the shelter was a rewarding experience.

mis.bad: The trip was rewarded.
mis.good: The trip was rewarding.
mis.why: "Rewarded" means given a prize; -ing describes an experience that satisfies you.

def: A university student studying for a first degree.
ex: As an undergraduate, he spent a year studying abroad.
nat: Most undergraduates live on campus in their first year.

mis.bad: I'm a graduate student; I'm in my second year of a bachelor's.
mis.good: I'm an undergraduate; I'm in my second year of a bachelor's.
mis.why: In US English, a graduate student is doing a master's or PhD; a bachelor's student is an undergraduate.

def: Harmful substances that damage air, water, or land.
ex: Air pollution is a serious problem in many big cities.
nat: Plastic pollution is killing sea animals around the world.

mis.bad: The pollution of the air is high.
mis.good: Air pollution is high.
mis.why: English uses the noun adjunct "air pollution" instead of "pollution of the air".

def: A large place where rubbish is buried.
ex: Most of our household waste ends up in a landfill.
nat: The old landfill outside town will close next year.

mis.bad: The garbage goes to the sanitary landfill.
mis.good: The garbage goes to a landfill.
mis.why: "Sanitary landfill" is a technical term; in everyday English just say "landfill".

def: Animals and plants living in natural conditions.
ex: The reserve protects wildlife from illegal hunting.
nat: We saw amazing wildlife on our safari.

mis.bad: The wildlifes of Brazil are diverse.
mis.good: The wildlife of Brazil is diverse.
mis.why: Wildlife is uncountable and has no plural.

def: At risk of disappearing completely.
ex: The golden lion tamarin is an endangered species.
nat: Many endangered animals live in this rainforest.

mis.bad: It is an extinction animal.
mis.good: It is an endangered animal.
mis.why: "Extinct" means already gone; an animal at risk is "endangered".

def: Able to continue without harming the environment.
ex: The company aims to use only sustainable materials by 2030.
nat: Fast fashion is not a sustainable way to dress.

mis.bad: It is a sustentable project.
mis.good: It is a sustainable project.
mis.why: The English form is "sustainable", not "sustentable".

def: Gases or substances released into the air.
ex: The city wants to cut carbon emissions by half within ten years.
nat: Car emissions are a major source of air pollution.

mis.bad: The emission of carbon is rising.
mis.good: Carbon emissions are rising.
mis.why: Use the plural "emissions" with a noun adjunct.

def: A long period with very little rain.
ex: The drought destroyed most of the crops last summer.
nat: Farmers are struggling after three years of drought.

mis.bad: The drought is a hot day.
mis.good: The drought lasted three months.
mis.why: Drought means a long lack of rain, not hot weather.

def: The cutting down of large areas of forest.
ex: Deforestation in the Amazon has slowed down in recent years.
nat: Illegal logging is the main cause of deforestation here.

mis.bad: The deforestation is growing in the Amazon.
mis.good: Deforestation is growing in the Amazon.
mis.why: No article before a general uncountable noun.

def: An unfair difference in wealth or opportunity.
ex: Income inequality has grown in many countries.
nat: The report highlights inequality in access to education.

mis.bad: The inequalities is big in Brazil.
mis.good: Inequality is big in Brazil.
mis.why: In this sense, inequality is usually uncountable.

def: The state of being very poor.
ex: Millions of people still live in poverty.
nat: She grew up in poverty but became a successful doctor.

mis.bad: They live in the poverty.
mis.good: They live in poverty.
mis.why: No article before "poverty" in this sense.

def: To offer to do something without being paid or forced.
ex: I volunteer at an animal shelter every Saturday.
nat: Nobody volunteered to clean the kitchen.

mis.bad: I made a voluntary work at the school.
mis.good: I do volunteer work at the school.
mis.why: Use "do volunteer work", not "make voluntary work".

def: To give money or goods to help others.
ex: Many people donated clothes after the flood.
nat: He donates part of his salary to charity every month.

mis.bad: She donated the charity some money.
mis.good: She donated some money to the charity.
mis.why: Donate cannot take two objects; use "to".

def: Unfair treatment of people because of who they are.
ex: The law bans discrimination based on age or gender.
nat: Many workers face discrimination because of their accent.

mis.bad: There is a lot of discrimination to women.
mis.good: There is a lot of discrimination against women.
mis.why: The preposition is "against".

def: The state of having no job.
ex: Youth unemployment is a major concern in the region.
nat: Unemployment fell to its lowest level in ten years.

mis.bad: The unemployment is high.
mis.good: Unemployment is high.
mis.why: No article before the general noun.

def: Worried and nervous about something uncertain.
ex: I felt anxious before my job interview.
nat: He is anxious about the test results.

mis.bad: I am anxious to go on vacation tomorrow.
mis.good: I am excited to go on vacation tomorrow.
mis.why: "Anxious" suggests worry, not simple excitement.

def: Having a strong wish to succeed.
ex: She is an ambitious young lawyer who wants to become a judge.
nat: They have ambitious plans to open ten new stores.

mis.bad: I am ambitious of becoming a manager.
mis.good: I am ambitious and want to become a manager.
mis.why: "Ambitious of" is not used; ambitious describes character.

def: Not confident about yourself.
ex: He felt insecure about his accent at first.
nat: Constant criticism can make anyone feel insecure.

mis.bad: I am insecure to walk at night.
mis.good: I feel unsafe walking at night.
mis.why: "Insecure" describes lack of confidence; for danger use "unsafe".

def: Showing care for other people's feelings.
ex: It was thoughtful of you to bring flowers.
nat: She sent a thoughtful message when I was sick.

mis.bad: It was very thoughtful from you.
mis.good: It was very thoughtful of you.
mis.why: Use "of you" after adjectives describing behavior (thoughtful, kind, nice).

def: Willing to give more than is expected.
ex: My uncle is generous and always pays for everyone.
nat: That's a very generous offer; thank you.

mis.bad: He is generous of money.
mis.good: He is generous with his money.
mis.why: Use "generous with" something.

def: Having moods that change quickly, often to bad ones.
ex: He gets moody when he doesn't sleep enough.
nat: Teenagers can be moody at times.

mis.bad: I am moody to travel.
mis.good: I am in the mood to travel.
mis.why: "Moody" means changeable in mood; the wish to do something is "in the mood for/to".

def: Relaxed and not easily upset.
ex: My boss is easygoing, so the office is a pleasant place.
nat: She is easygoing and gets along with everyone.

mis.bad: She is very easy going with everyone.
mis.good: She is very easygoing with everyone.
mis.why: It is one word (or hyphenated: easy-going), not two.

def: Caring only about yourself.
ex: It was selfish of him to take the last piece without asking.
nat: Don't be selfish; share your toys.

mis.bad: He is very selfish person.
mis.good: He is a very selfish person.
mis.why: Singular countable nouns need an article.

def: Not proud and not thinking you are better than others.
ex: Despite his fame, he stays humble and kind.
nat: She comes from a humble background.

mis.bad: He is very humiliated about his success.
mis.good: He is very humble about his success.
mis.why: "Humiliated" means shamed by others; "humble" (humilde) means modest.

def: Sad because something was not as good as you hoped.
ex: I was disappointed with the final episode of the series.
nat: They were disappointed that the concert was cancelled.

mis.bad: I am disappointed of you.
mis.good: I am disappointed with you.
mis.why: Use "with" or "in" after disappointed, not "of".

def: Happy because something bad did not happen.
ex: I was so relieved when the test results came back negative.
nat: She looked relieved to hear that everyone was safe.

mis.bad: I'm very relief that you are safe.
mis.good: I'm very relieved that you are safe.
mis.why: Use the adjective "relieved", not the noun "relief".

def: Feeling awkward or ashamed in front of others.
ex: I felt embarrassed when I forgot his name.
nat: He was too embarrassed to ask for help.

mis.bad: I was embarassed because I forgot his name.
mis.good: I was embarrassed because I forgot his name.
mis.why: Mind the spelling: double r and double s. Also, it never means "pregnant", unlike "embaraçada".

def: Very excited and interested in something.
ex: The students were enthusiastic about the new project.
nat: He wasn't very enthusiastic about moving to another city.

mis.bad: She is enthusiastic of the idea.
mis.good: She is enthusiastic about the idea.
mis.why: Use "about" after enthusiastic.

def: Annoyed because you have to wait or because things are slow.
ex: I get impatient when the line moves slowly.
nat: He was impatient to start the new job.

mis.bad: She is impatient for her kids.
mis.good: She is impatient with her kids.
mis.why: Use "impatient with" a person.

def: Showing that you understand and care about someone's problems.
ex: My manager was sympathetic when I explained my situation.
nat: She gave me a sympathetic smile.

mis.bad: He is very sympathetic with everybody, always smiling.
mis.good: He is very friendly with everybody, always smiling.
mis.why: "Sympathetic" means understanding of suffering; "simpático" is "nice" or "friendly".

def: To delay doing something that you should do.
ex: I always procrastinate when I have to write reports.
nat: Stop procrastinating and start your homework.

mis.bad: I procrastinated to study.
mis.good: I procrastinated instead of studying.
mis.why: Procrastinate is intransitive and is not followed by "to + verb".

def: The practice of paying full attention to the present moment.
ex: Ten minutes of mindfulness each morning helps me stay calm.
nat: She teaches mindfulness at a local clinic.

mis.bad: I practice a mindfulness every day.
mis.good: I practice mindfulness every day.
mis.why: Mindfulness is uncountable.

def: The usual way you do things every day.
ex: My morning routine includes a short walk and a cup of coffee.
nat: Travelling disrupted my sleep routine.

mis.bad: I have a busy routine of work.
mis.good: I have a busy daily routine.
mis.why: The usual phrase is "daily routine".

pt: distração, o que desvia a atenção
def: Something that takes your attention away from what you are doing.
ex: My phone is the biggest distraction when I study.
nat: Turn off the TV; it's a distraction.

mis.bad: I am a distraction person, I forget everything.
mis.good: I am easily distracted, so I forget things.
mis.why: "Distraction" is something that diverts attention; it does not describe a personality.

def: How much you value yourself.
ex: Positive feedback can raise a child's self-esteem.
nat: Social media can damage teenagers' self-esteem.

mis.bad: I have a low self-esteem.
mis.good: I have low self-esteem.
mis.why: Self-esteem is uncountable: no article.

def: To think too much about something so that it causes stress.
ex: Stop overthinking; it was just a short message.
nat: I tend to overthink small decisions.

mis.bad: I overthink too much about everything.
mis.good: I overthink everything.
mis.why: The prefix "over-" already means "too much".

def: To relax after a period of work or stress.
ex: I like to unwind with a book after a long day.
nat: We went to the beach to unwind for the weekend.

mis.bad: I unwinded on the sofa.
mis.good: I unwound on the sofa.
mis.why: The past of unwind is irregular: unwound.

def: Extremely tired.
ex: After the long flight, I was completely exhausted.
nat: She looked exhausted after working two shifts.

mis.bad: I am exhausting after work.
mis.good: I am exhausted after work.
mis.why: Use -ed for how you feel; "exhausting" describes what causes it.

def: To say or do something that makes someone feel less worried.
ex: The doctor reassured her that the test was routine.
nat: His calm voice reassured the nervous passengers.

mis.bad: He reassured me to not worry.
mis.good: He reassured me that there was nothing to worry about.
mis.why: Reassure takes an object plus "that + clause", not "to + verb".

def: The ability to control yourself and keep doing something.
ex: Learning a language takes discipline, not just talent.
nat: He has the discipline to train every morning.

mis.bad: I study discipline English at school.
mis.good: I study English as a subject at school.
mis.why: "Discipline" means self-control or order; a school subject is better called "subject".

def: A message from an app or phone telling you something new happened.
ex: I turned off notifications so I could focus on my work.
nat: You'll get a notification when your order ships.

mis.bad: I received a notification of the app.
mis.good: I received a notification from the app.
mis.why: The sender is introduced with "from".

def: A regular payment to receive a service or product.
ex: I cancelled my streaming subscription because I never used it.
nat: A yearly subscription is cheaper than paying monthly.

mis.bad: I made a signature of the magazine.
mis.good: I took out a subscription to the magazine.
mis.why: "Signature" is a handwritten name; for a service, use "subscription".

def: Watching or listening online without downloading.
ex: Streaming has changed the way people watch films.
nat: Most of my friends use streaming services instead of cable TV.

mis.bad: I watch series in streaming.
mis.good: I watch series on a streaming service.
mis.why: English does not say "in streaming"; use "streaming service" or the verb "stream".

def: The title of a news story, usually in large letters.
ex: The headline made the story sound far worse than it was.
nat: I only read the headlines on my phone each morning.

mis.bad: The newspaper's head was misleading.
mis.good: The newspaper's headline was misleading.
mis.why: A news title is a "headline", not a "head".

def: A person who affects what others buy or do through social media.
ex: The brand paid an influencer to promote its new sneakers.
nat: My cousin wants to become a full-time influencer.

mis.bad: She is a digital influencer.
mis.good: She is a social media influencer.
mis.why: "Digital influencer" is a Portuguese pattern; English says "social media influencer" or just "influencer".

def: Spreading very quickly on the internet.
ex: The video went viral and got ten million views in a day.
nat: A viral post turned the small bakery into a local celebrity.

mis.bad: The video became viral.
mis.good: The video went viral.
mis.why: The natural collocation is "go viral".

def: Making you want to do or use something again and again.
ex: This game is so addictive that I lose track of time.
nat: Sugar can be as addictive as some drugs, researchers say.

mis.bad: This game is very vicious.
mis.good: This game is very addictive.
mis.why: "Viciante" is "addictive"; "vicious" means cruel or violent.

def: False information shared without necessarily meaning to deceive.
ex: Misinformation spread quickly during the election.
nat: Always check the source to avoid sharing misinformation.

mis.bad: There are many misinformations online.
mis.good: There is a lot of misinformation online.
mis.why: Misinformation is uncountable.

def: To move text or images up and down on a screen.
ex: I scrolled through my feed for an hour without noticing.
nat: Scroll down to see the full list of prices.

mis.bad: I made scroll on the page.
mis.good: I scrolled down the page.
mis.why: Scroll is a verb itself; do not use "make scroll".

def: To look at things online or in a shop without a fixed aim.
ex: I browsed the website for an hour before buying anything.
nat: I like to browse in bookstores on Saturdays.

mis.bad: I navigate on the internet every night.
mis.good: I browse the internet every night.
mis.why: "Navigate" is for finding your way; for casual web use, say "browse".

def: A small problem that stops something from working properly.
ex: A software glitch delayed all flights this morning.
nat: There was a glitch in the video, so it kept freezing.

mis.bad: The system had a glitch of connection.
mis.good: The system had a connection glitch.
mis.why: Put the noun before "glitch" (a connection glitch) instead of using "of".

def: To disconnect a device from the power, or to take a break from technology.
ex: I unplugged the router and waited a minute before restarting it.
nat: We go to a cabin every summer to unplug from our phones.

mis.bad: Please unplug the light.
mis.good: Please turn off the light.
mis.why: Unplug means to pull a plug from a socket; lights are turned off.

def: The control of what people can say, read, or see.
ex: The government introduced strict censorship of the press.
nat: Online censorship makes it hard to get honest news.

mis.bad: There is a censorship in that country.
mis.good: There is censorship in that country.
mis.why: Censorship is uncountable.

def: A person who writes or reports news.
ex: The journalist interviewed several witnesses about the accident.
nat: My sister is a journalist for a local newspaper.

mis.bad: She works as a journalist in the journal of the city.
mis.good: She works as a journalist for the city newspaper.
mis.why: False friend: "journal" is a specialist or academic publication; a daily is a "newspaper" (jornal).

def: To give money to support an event or team in return for advertising.
ex: A local bank sponsors the youth football team.
nat: The festival is sponsored by several large companies.

mis.bad: The company patronizes the festival.
mis.good: The company sponsors the festival.
mis.why: "Patronize" means to treat someone as inferior; use "sponsor" for funding.

def: To watch and direct people or work to make sure it is done well.
ex: She supervises a team of twelve technicians.
nat: A teacher must supervise the students on the trip.

mis.bad: I supervise to the team.
mis.good: I supervise the team.
mis.why: Supervise is transitive, with no preposition.

def: To organize different people or tasks so they work well together.
ex: Someone has to coordinate the schedules of all the speakers.
nat: He coordinates volunteers at the city's food bank.

mis.bad: She coordinates to the project.
mis.good: She coordinates the project.
mis.why: Coordinate is transitive; use "coordinate with" only for working together with someone.

def: To produce many ideas quickly in a group.
ex: We brainstormed names for the new product for an hour.
nat: Let's brainstorm some solutions before the meeting ends.

mis.bad: We made a brainstorm to find ideas.
mis.good: We brainstormed ideas.
mis.why: Brainstorm is mainly a verb; as a noun say "brainstorming session".

def: Comments about how well someone is doing.
ex: My manager gave me useful feedback on the report.
nat: We welcome feedback from our customers.

mis.bad: I got many feedbacks from my boss.
mis.good: I got a lot of feedback from my boss.
mis.why: Feedback is uncountable.

def: To work together to achieve something.
ex: The two departments need to cooperate to solve this issue.
nat: The suspect refused to cooperate with the police.

mis.bad: We cooperate to each other.
mis.good: We cooperate with each other.
mis.why: Cooperate takes "with".

def: An opinion that all members of a group agree on.
ex: After a long discussion, the team reached a consensus.
nat: There is no consensus among scientists on this issue.

mis.bad: We made a consensus.
mis.good: We reached a consensus.
mis.why: The collocation is "reach" (or "build") a consensus.

def: The ability to start something without being told.
ex: She took the initiative and organized the training herself.
nat: He shows a lot of initiative for a new employee.

mis.bad: She made the initiative to start the project.
mis.good: She took the initiative to start the project.
mis.why: Use "take the initiative", not "make".

def: To make someone want to do something.
ex: A good leader knows how to motivate the team.
nat: Money alone doesn't motivate most people.

mis.bad: She is very motivate.
mis.good: She is very motivated.
mis.why: Use the adjective "motivated".

def: To give people the confidence or authority to make decisions.
ex: Good managers empower their staff to solve problems on their own.
nat: The program empowers women to start their own businesses.

mis.bad: The company empowers to employees.
mis.good: The company empowers employees.
mis.why: Empower is transitive: no "to" before the object.

def: To control every small detail of other people's work.
ex: Our boss micromanages everything, so nobody feels trusted.
nat: I hate it when someone micromanages me.

mis.bad: My boss is very micromanage.
mis.good: My boss is a micromanager.
mis.why: Micromanage is a verb; the person is a "micromanager".

def: Praise or credit given for good work.
ex: She finally received recognition for her years of hard work.
nat: Employees need recognition to stay motivated.

mis.bad: He got recognition of the boss.
mis.good: He got recognition from the boss.
mis.why: Use "from" for the source of the recognition.

def: To weaken something gradually.
ex: Constant gossip can undermine trust within a team.
nat: His rude comments undermined my confidence.

mis.bad: Gossip undermines to the team.
mis.good: Gossip undermines the team.
mis.why: Undermine is transitive: no preposition before the object.

def: To give something, such as ideas or money, to help achieve something.
ex: Everyone contributed ideas during the workshop.
nat: Stress contributes to many health problems.

mis.bad: He contributed for the project.
mis.good: He contributed to the project.
mis.why: Use "to" after contribute.

def: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other.
ex: The new coach quickly built rapport with the players.
nat: Good rapport with clients can lead to repeat business.

mis.bad: I have a good rapport of him.
mis.good: I have a good rapport with him.
mis.why: Use "rapport with" a person.

def: A serious disagreement between people or groups.
ex: The two neighbors are in a long dispute over the fence.
nat: A pay dispute led to a strike at the factory.

mis.bad: The two teams are in a dispute for the title.
mis.good: The two teams are competing for the title.
mis.why: "Disputa" can mean competition; English "dispute" is a disagreement or argument.

def: A piece of paper that shows you paid for something.
ex: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the shirt.
nat: Can I have the receipt, please?

mis.bad: Can you give me the recipe of the purchase?
mis.good: Can I have the receipt?
mis.why: Recipe is for cooking; the paper for a purchase is a receipt.

def: A lower price than normal.
ex: They gave us a ten percent discount for paying in cash.
nat: Students get a discount at the cinema.

mis.bad: They made a discount of ten percent to me.
mis.good: They gave me a ten percent discount.
mis.why: The natural verbs are "give" or "offer" a discount.

def: A promise by a company to repair a product if it breaks.
ex: The laptop comes with a two-year warranty.
nat: The warranty expired last month, so we have to pay for repairs.

mis.bad: The product has a garantee of two years.
mis.good: The product has a two-year warranty.
mis.why: For a product, "warranty" is more common than "guarantee".

def: A person who takes payment in a shop.
ex: The cashier gave me the wrong change.
nat: Please pay the cashier on your way out.

mis.bad: I paid in the cashier.
mis.good: I paid the cashier.
mis.why: You pay a person; at the till you say "at the checkout".

def: Costing more than it is worth.
ex: The food was good but overpriced for such a small portion.
nat: I think these sneakers are overpriced.

mis.bad: This shirt is too much expensive.
mis.good: This shirt is overpriced.
mis.why: "Too much" is not used before an adjective; say "too expensive" or "overpriced".

def: A person who owns a property and rents it to others.
ex: Our landlord is fixing the heating this week.
nat: I pay my rent to the landlord on the first of each month.

mis.bad: My proprietary raised the rent.
mis.good: My landlord raised the rent.
mis.why: "Proprietary" means owned by a company; the person who rents out a home is a "landlord".

def: A person who pays rent to live in or use a property.
ex: The tenant complained about the broken elevator.
nat: The tenants have to leave by the end of June.

mis.bad: He is a tenent in my building.
mis.good: He is a tenant in my building.
mis.why: Spelling: tenant ends in -ant.

def: To pay money regularly to use a house, flat, or car.
ex: We rent a small apartment close to the subway.
nat: Many young people can't afford to buy a house, so they rent.

mis.bad: The rent of a car costs a lot.
mis.good: Renting a car costs a lot.
mis.why: As a noun, "rent" is the regular payment for housing; for the action use the verb or "car rental".

def: Having furniture already inside.
ex: They found a furnished apartment near the university.
nat: The flat is fully furnished, so you only need to bring clothes.

mis.bad: I'm looking for a furnitured apartment.
mis.good: I'm looking for a furnished apartment.
mis.why: The adjective is "furnished" (from furnish), not "furnitured".

def: To repair and improve an old building.
ex: They renovated the old house before moving in.
nat: We plan to renovate the kitchen next spring.

mis.bad: I am doing a reform in my house.
mis.good: I am renovating my house.
mis.why: "Reform" in English means to change laws or behavior, not to renovate a building.

def: A machine used at home, such as a fridge or washing machine.
ex: Most kitchen appliances are cheaper during the holiday sales.
nat: This appliance uses a lot of electricity.

mis.bad: I bought a new electrodomestic.
mis.good: I bought a new appliance.
mis.why: The English word is "appliance".

def: A part of a town where people live.
ex: It is a quiet neighborhood with lots of parks.
nat: We moved to a nicer neighborhood last year.

mis.bad: I live in the neighborhood Savassi.
mis.good: I live in the Savassi neighborhood.
mis.why: English puts the name before "neighborhood"; Portuguese puts "bairro" first.

def: An area outside the center of a city where people live.
ex: They live in a green suburb about twenty minutes from downtown.
nat: Many families move to the suburbs for more space.

mis.bad: I live in a poor suburb with no buildings.
mis.good: I live in a suburb outside the city.
mis.why: In English, suburbs are often comfortable residential areas, not necessarily poor.

def: A person walking rather than driving.
ex: A car hit a pedestrian near the crossing.
nat: The street is closed to traffic and open only to pedestrians.

mis.bad: The pedestrian cross is closed.
mis.good: The pedestrian crossing is closed.
mis.why: The phrase is "pedestrian crossing" (US: crosswalk).

def: In or toward the main business area of a city.
ex: I work downtown, so I take the subway every day.
nat: We went downtown for dinner and a movie.

mis.bad: I live in the downtown of the city.
mis.good: I live downtown.
mis.why: "Downtown" is usually an adverb or adjective in American English.

def: More and more as time goes on.
ex: Increasingly, cities are banning single-use plastic bags.
nat: Remote work is increasingly common in my industry.

mis.bad: Each time more people work from home.
mis.good: Increasingly, more people work from home.
mis.why: "Cada vez mais" is "increasingly" or "more and more", not "each time more".
